pumac-2016-algebra-b-03.title: Write the new equation
pumac-2016-algebra-b-03.body:
Moving the origin to $(-20,16)$ means the curve in new coordinates is $y=(x-20)^3-13(x-20)^2+40(x-20)+25-16$. The sum of the roots of a monic cubic is minus the $x^2$ coefficient: the $x^2$ coefficient is $-3\cdot20-13=-73$, so the sum is $73$.

**Answer: 73**

pumac-2016-algebra-b-03.title: Shift the roots
pumac-2016-algebra-b-03.body:
Changing the constant term does not change the sum of the roots of the original cubic, which is $13$. Translating the graph $20$ to the right adds $20$ to each of the three roots, so the sum becomes $13+60=73$.

**Answer: 73**

pumac-2016-algebra-b-04.title: Linear equation
pumac-2016-algebra-b-04.body:
$f^5(x)=f(x)$ is a linear equation in $x$ (the coefficient of $x$ is $15^5-15\ne0$), so it has exactly one solution. Any fixed point of $f$ satisfies it, and $f(x)=x$ gives $14x=2016$, $x=144$. So $144$ is the only solution and the sum is $144$.

**Answer: 144**

pumac-2016-algebra-b-05.title: Turn it into a cubic in $\log_2 x$
pumac-2016-algebra-b-05.body:
$f(x,x)=x^{\log_2 x}$ and $f(f(x,x),x)=\left(x^{\log_2 x}\right)^{\log_2 x}=x^{(\log_2 x)^2}$. Let $t=\log_2x$. The equation becomes $2^{12}\cdot2^{t\cdot t^2}=2^{13t}$, i.e. $t^3-13t+12=0$, which factors as $(t-1)(t-3)(t+4)=0$.

So $x=2,\,8,\,\frac1{16}$, with sum $\frac{161}{16}$ and $m+n=161+16=177$.

**Answer: 177**

pumac-2016-algebra-b-06.title: Divisibility and CRT
pumac-2016-algebra-b-06.body:
For an integer polynomial, $x_1-x_2\mid P(x_1)-P(x_2)$. With $x_1=2016$ and $x_2=1,2,3$ we get $N\equiv2\pmod{2015}$, $N\equiv3\pmod{2014}$, $N\equiv2016\equiv3\pmod{2013}$.

The moduli $2013=3\cdot11\cdot61$, $2014=2\cdot19\cdot53$, $2015=5\cdot13\cdot31$ are pairwise coprime, so $P(2016)$ is determined mod $2013\cdot2014\cdot2015$. The number $3+1007\cdot2013\cdot2014$ works: it is $3$ mod $2013$ and mod $2014$, and mod $2015$ it is $3+1007\cdot(-2)(-1)=3+2014\equiv2$. It lies between $0$ and $2013\cdot2014\cdot2015$, so it is the smallest positive possibility.

It is attained: $P(x)=(x-1)\big(1006(x-2)+1\big)+2$ has $P(1)=2$, $P(2)=3$, $P(3)=2016$ and $P(2016)=2015\cdot(2014\cdot1006+1)+2=3+1007\cdot2013\cdot2014$.

Modulo $2016$: $2013\equiv-3$, $2014\equiv-2$, so $N\equiv3+1007\cdot6=6045\equiv2013$.

**Answer: 2013**

pumac-2016-algebra-b-07.title: Track numbers of the form $2^k-1$
pumac-2016-algebra-b-07.body:
$a_2=181^2-1=32760=8\cdot4095$, so $a_3,a_4,a_5=16380,8190,4095=2^{12}-1$.

If $a_i=2^k-1$ (odd), then $a_{i+1}=(2^k-1)^2-1=2^{k+1}(2^{k-1}-1)$, and halving $k+1$ times gives $a_{i+k+2}=2^{k-1}-1$. So passing from $2^k-1$ to $2^{k-1}-1$ takes $k+2$ terms, except for $k=1$: $a_i=1$ gives $a_{i+1}=0$ in just one step.

Starting from $a_5$ ($k=12$) down to $k=2$ costs $\sum_{k=2}^{12}(k+2)=77+22=99$ terms, reaching $a_{104}=2^1-1=1$, and then $a_{105}=0$.

**Answer: 105**

pumac-2016-algebra-b-08.title: Find all solutions
pumac-2016-algebra-b-08.body:
Write $P(x)=\prod(x-\alpha_i)$. Comparing root multisets in $P(x^2)=P(x)P(x-1)$ gives $\{\pm\sqrt{\alpha_i}\}=\{\alpha_i\}\cup\{\alpha_i+1\}$. If some $|\alpha_i|>1$ the largest modulus $M^2$ on the left would exceed $M$ on the right; similarly no nonzero $|\alpha_i|<1$ (and $0$ cannot be a root since its multiplicities on both sides differ). So all roots satisfy $|\alpha|=|\alpha+1|=1$, i.e. $\alpha=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt3 i}{2}$, and the two roots have equal multiplicity.

Hence $P(x)=(x^2+x+1)^n$, or $P=0$, or $P=1$. Then $P(1)=3^n$ must divide $2016=2^5\cdot3^2\cdot7$, so $n\le2$. Thus $P_0(x)=(x^2+x+1)^2$ and $P_0(10)=111^2=12321$.

**Answer: 12321**
